A bespoke suit is built in stages and checked on your body between them. Across the trade, the whole ascent typically takes 6–12 weeks. See the full process . 01 Consultation 60–90 minutes We start with how you work, travel and present, and what the suit needs to do. Then we agree on the style, the occasion and a budget. 02 Measurements Taken at the consultation Twenty-plus measurements, plus posture notes a tape measure can't capture: shoulder slope, stance, seat and the way you carry your arms. 03 Fabric Same visit or a follow-up You choose from cloth books from [PLACEHOLDER: fabric mills / merchants carried, e.g. Holland & Sherry, Loro Piana, Vitale Barberis Canonico, Dormeuil ] , guided by season, weight, Utah's climate and how often you'll wear it. 04 Construction [PLACEHOLDER: construction lead time in weeks ] The pattern is cut and the suit is built in stages, with fittings along the way so the shape is refined on your body rather than on paper. 05 Final Fitting 45 minutes We check balance, sleeve pitch, collar and trouser break in natural light and while you move. Then the suit is pressed and handed over with care instructions. Anatomy of the Suit What you are paying for is mostly invisible . The difference between a good suit and a great one sits under the cloth: the canvas, the shoulder, the hand work. Here is what to look for in any jacket, ours included. 01 The Canvas Full canvas, half canvas or fused A layer of wool and horsehair between the cloth and the lining gives the jacket its shape. A full canvas runs the whole front and floats free, so it moulds to your chest over time. A half canvas covers the chest and lapel. A fused front is glued, which is cheaper and flatter, and can blister after dry cleaning. 02 The Lapel Notch, peak or shawl, with a hand-padded roll Lapel width should follow your shoulders and face. Around 3 to 3¾ inches suits most frames. Padding the lapel by hand with hundreds of small stitches gives it a soft, three-dimensional roll instead of a pressed-flat crease. 03 The Shoulder The one part that can't be altered later The shoulder sets how a jacket hangs. It can be soft and natural, or built up with a light pad and roped sleeve head. It is cut to your own shoulder slope, which is why off-the-rack jackets so often fail here first. 04 Buttons & Stance The top button sets your waistline Button stance, the height of the fastening button, defines where the eye reads your waist. Setting it slightly above the natural waist lengthens the leg line. Horn, corozo and mother-of-pearl are the classic materials. 05 Pockets Flap, jetted or patch, by formality Jetted pockets are the most formal and suit dinner and wedding suits. Flap pockets are the business standard. Patch pockets relax a jacket for odd jackets and weekend tailoring. A ticket pocket adds a Savile Row accent. 06 The Lining Cupro breathes; polyester doesn't Bemberg cupro, a regenerated cotton fibre, wicks moisture and slides on and off smoothly. That matters in a dry Utah summer. Half or quarter linings lighten warm-weather jackets further. Image Consulting The suit is the instrument. Image is how you play it. /journal/bespoke-vs-made-to-measure-vs-o.text: Home / Journal / Bespoke vs Made-to-Measure vs Off-the-Rack: What You're Actually Paying For Tailoring Bespoke vs Made-to-Measure vs Off-the-Rack: What You're Actually Paying For By [PLACEHOLDER: founder full name ] , Founder & Head Clothier · October 19, 2026 · 9 min read In this article The pattern is the product Off-the-rack Made-to-measure Bespoke Inside the jacket Side by side Price versus cost per wear When “bespoke” isn't bespoke How to choose Key takeaways Bespoke = a pattern drafted from scratch for you, refined over typically 3+ fittings, 6–12 weeks. Made-to-measure = a factory block pattern adjusted to your measurements, usually 3–6 weeks and 1 fitting. Off-the-rack = standard sizes, altered afterwards. The shoulder can't be fixed. Most of the price difference is hidden: canvas construction and hours of hand work. Three suits can hang side by side in navy worsted, each with two buttons and notch lapels, and still differ in price by a factor of ten. The label tells you very little. What you are paying for is mostly invisible: how the pattern was made, what is inside the jacket, and how many times a skilled person checked it on your body before it was finished. Here is what the three categories actually mean, and how to decide which one you need. The pattern is the product Every suit begins as a paper pattern, the flat shapes that are traced onto cloth and cut. The single most important question about any suit is whose pattern was it? An off-the-rack suit uses a standard pattern graded into sizes, such as 40R or 42L. A made-to-measure suit uses the same kind of standard pattern (a “block”), adjusted to your measurements. A bespoke suit uses a pattern drafted from nothing, for you alone. Everything else (price, timeline, how many fittings you need, how good it looks after five years) follows from that one difference. Off-the-rack: fast, affordable, built for an average Ready-to-wear suits are cut for a statistical average body in each size. If you match the average, a good off-the-rack suit with sensible alterations can look sharp. The trouble is that very few people match it. Athletic builds, long torsos, sloping or square shoulders, or one shoulder lower than the other all fall outside the block. Alterations can shorten sleeves, hem trousers and take in a waist. They cannot fix the shoulder, the chest or the balance of the jacket (how the front and back hang relative to each other). Those are the things that make a suit look like it belongs to you. Typical timeline: same day, plus about a week for alterations. Typical US price: $200–$1,500. Made-to-measure: a better starting point Made-to-measure (MTM) takes a factory block pattern and adjusts it: longer sleeves, a shorter jacket, more room in the seat. Often you choose from a menu of styles and cloths, and the garment is produced by a factory, typically abroad. Good MTM is a real step up from off-the-rack, especially for people who are simply longer or shorter than standard. Its limit is the block. Adjustments are made to a shape designed for someone else, so complex posture issues are approximated rather than solved. Most MTM programmes include a single fitting when the finished garment arrives, with alterations from there. Typical timeline: 3–6 weeks. Typical US price: $800–$2,500. Bespoke: a pattern that belongs to you The word comes from the old Savile Row practice of a cloth being “spoken for” by a particular customer. A bespoke tailor measures you, studies your posture and drafts a pattern from a blank sheet. The suit is cut and loosely basted together, then fitted on your body. It is often taken apart, recut and fitted again. The trade standard is three fittings: Baste fitting: the jacket is tacked together with white thread and has no finished edges. Shape and balance are corrected here. Forward fitting: the sleeves and collar are set and the shape is confirmed. Final fitting: details, sleeve length and trouser break, before the last pressing. Because the pattern is yours, it is kept on file. The second suit starts from a proven fit, and is often faster. Typical timeline: 6–12 weeks. Typical US price: $3,000–$8,000 and up, depending on cloth and hand work. Inside the jacket: canvas, fused and the hours you can’t see Between the outer cloth and the lining sits the jacket’s structure. How it is built is the second-largest driver of price, after the pattern. Fused: an adhesive interlining is heat-bonded to the cloth. It is fast and inexpensive, and it can produce a flat, slightly stiff front that may blister after repeated dry cleaning. Half canvas: a floating wool–horsehair canvas runs through the chest and lapel, with a fused lower front. It is a sound middle ground and common in better MTM. Full canvas: the canvas runs the full length of the front and is attached with thousands of small stitches. It moulds to your chest with wear and lets the lapel roll naturally. It is standard in traditional bespoke. Add hand-padded lapels, a hand-set collar and hand-sewn buttonholes, and a traditional bespoke jacket can carry dozens of hours of skilled hand work. That labour is most of what the price buys. Side by side Typical figures across the US market. Individual makers vary. Attribute Bespoke Made-to-measure Off-the-rack Pattern Drafted from scratch for you A stock block pattern, adjusted Standard sizes Fittings Typically 3 or more Usually 1, at the end None (alterations only) Posture & asymmetry Corrected in the pattern Partly corrected Not corrected Construction Usually full canvas, hand finished Half canvas or fused, machine made Mostly fused Typical timeline 6–12 weeks 3–6 weeks Same day + alterations Typical US price $3,000–$8,000+ $800–$2,500 $200–$1,500 Price versus cost per wear Sticker price is the wrong number to compare. What matters is cost per wear. Suppose a well-made bespoke suit is worn twice a week for eight years and rotated with other suits. That is roughly 800 wears. A fused off-the-rack suit worn the same way often shows its age within two or three years: a bubbling chest, shiny seat, collapsed shoulder. It has to be replaced, and the replacement is altered again. Bespoke also keeps its value through change. Traditional bespoke trousers and jackets are built with generous inlays , extra cloth folded into the seams, so they can be let out or taken in when your body changes. Mass-produced garments rarely have more than a sliver of seam allowance. None of this makes bespoke the right answer for everyone. For a suit you’ll wear a handful of times, a good off-the-rack suit with careful alterations is sensible. For the suits that carry your working life, the arithmetic usually favours building them properly once. When “bespoke” isn’t bespoke In the United States, “bespoke” is not a protected term. Plenty of made-to-measure programmes use it in their marketing. Five questions sort one from the other: Is my pattern drafted from scratch, or adjusted from a block? Only the first is bespoke. Will there be a baste fitting? A garment tacked together for fitting before it is finished is the hallmark of bespoke. How many fittings are included? One fitting at the end is the made-to-measure model. What is the construction? Ask directly whether the front is full canvas, half canvas or fused. Who cuts, and where is it made? Knowing who drafts your pattern and where the garment is sewn tells you a great deal. A good maker, bespoke or made-to-measure, will answer all five plainly. Neither is a lesser product when it’s sold honestly. They are simply different. How to choose Ask three questions: How often will you wear it? A suit worn three days a week for years justifies bespoke construction. One worn twice a year may not. How standard is your build? If off-the-rack jackets always fail at the shoulder or chest, MTM will help a little and bespoke will help a lot. What is the suit for? For a wedding, a trial or a public role, being seen at your best for hours is worth the investment. Summit Customs specialises in bespoke. /journal/custom-wedding-suit-timeline.text: Home / Journal / Custom Wedding Suit Timeline: When to Start and What to Expect Weddings Custom Wedding Suit Timeline: When to Start and What to Expect By [PLACEHOLDER: founder full name ] , Founder & Head Clothier · October 19, 2026 · 8 min read In this article The short answer Month by month Dressing the party Utah venues and seasons Choosing the style Budgeting Accessories checklist After the wedding Common mistakes Questions to ask your tailor If you're short on time Key takeaways Start 4–6 months before the wedding; 6 months if you're dressing the whole party. Schedule the final fitting 2–3 weeks before the day, not earlier. Utah's peak wedding season (May–October) fills tailoring calendars early. Choose cloth for the venue: mid-weight for mountain evenings, high-twist for valley summers. A custom wedding suit is made in stages, with fittings in between, so it cannot be rushed the way a rental can. The good news is that the timeline is predictable. Start at the right point, and your final fitting lands comfortably in the last few weeks before the day. The short answer Start four to six months before your wedding. If you are coordinating suits for groomsmen and fathers, start at six months. Schedule your final fitting two to three weeks before the date , close enough to reflect any change in weight or training, and far enough out to allow one last adjustment. Month by month Six months out: consultation and measurements Your first appointment is a conversation about the day: the venue, the season, the time of the ceremony, the formality and the photographs. Then come measurements and posture notes, from which your pattern is drafted. If the wedding party is being coordinated, this is the time to set the brief for everyone. Five months out: cloth, colour and details Cloth is chosen against the venue and season, the wedding’s palette and the light it will be photographed in. Lapel style, button stance, pockets, lining and buttons are agreed now. A midnight-navy dinner suit for an evening reception and a light high-twist suit for a July garden ceremony are very different commissions. Four months out: the baste fitting The jacket is loosely tacked together so the tailor can correct shape and balance on your body. It is the most important fitting, and it looks the least finished. Two to three months out: the forward fitting Sleeves and collar are set and the trousers are refined. Bring your wedding shoes so the trouser break is right. Two to three weeks out: the final fitting The last check. Sleeve length, trouser break and any final adjustment are made. Accessories (tie or bow tie, pocket square, cufflinks, braces) are confirmed against the finished suit. Wedding week: collection The suit is pressed and collected. Hang it on a broad, shaped hanger, away from direct sun, and don’t try it on again until the morning. Dressing the wedding party A coordinated party looks considered, not uniform. Common approaches are the same cloth with the groom in a waistcoat or a different lapel, or a shared colour family across different cloths. Out-of-town groomsmen need to be measured early, because their fittings are hardest to schedule. Summit Customs process for remote party members: [PLACEHOLDER: remote measuring process for out-of-town clients and groomsmen ] . Utah venues and seasons Utah’s wedding season runs mainly May through October, and its venues range from valley ballrooms to ski-resort decks above 8,000 feet. Plan the cloth for the place: Mountain ceremonies (Park City, Deer Valley, the Cottonwood canyons): strong sun and cool evenings, often 20°F or more colder after sunset. Mid-weight wool at 260–300 g handles both. Valley summer receptions (Salt Lake City, Sandy, Draper, Provo): afternoons often pass 95°F in July. High-twist wool, fresco or wool–linen at 230–270 g. Temple sealings: the suit is typically worn for arrival, exterior photographs and the reception or ring ceremony. A classic cut will photograph well for decades. Winter weddings: flannel or a heavier worsted, plus an overcoat for exterior photographs in the snow. Choosing the style The formality of the day decides the garment. The garment then decides the timeline and the budget. Lounge suit (two-piece): the most versatile choice for daytime and semi-formal weddings, and the one you are most likely to wear again. Navy, mid-grey and soft earth tones photograph well outdoors. Three-piece suit: adds a waistcoat that keeps you looking finished once the jacket comes off for the reception. It is very practical at a warm valley venue. Dinner suit (tuxedo): correct for black-tie evenings. Midnight navy or black, with a silk-faced peak or shawl lapel, braces rather than a belt, and a bow tie you tie yourself. Odd jacket and trousers: a relaxed option for small outdoor ceremonies and destination weekends, such as a textured jacket in a tone that complements the wedding party. Budgeting for the suit Plan your budget around three variables: the cloth, the construction and the number of garments. A waistcoat or a second pair of trousers adds to the commission but extends the suit’s life after the wedding. At Summit Customs, the groom’s custom suit starts at [PLACEHOLDER: groom's custom suit starting price ] , and the quote is confirmed in writing before cutting. Leave room for accessories: shoes, shirt, tie or bow tie, cufflinks and a pocket square. Accessories checklist Shirt: a fitted white or pale-blue shirt. A wing or turndown collar for black tie. Neckwear: tie or bow tie, chosen against the finished suit, not the swatch. Shoes: broken in before the day, and brought to every fitting. Socks: over-the-calf, in a colour that matches the trousers, so no shin shows when seated. Pocket square, cufflinks, braces and a watch that sits under the shirt cuff. Boutonnière: coordinate the colour and pin placement with your florist. After the wedding A well-chosen wedding suit should not hang unworn. If you choose a classic colour and a cut that suits you, it becomes the best suit in your wardrobe for anniversaries, other weddings and important meetings. Your pattern stays on file, so every future commission starts from a proven fit. Common mistakes Starting too late. Peak-season calendars fill. Under eight weeks narrows your options. Final fitting too early. A fitting two months out misses any change from pre-wedding training. Choosing cloth for the showroom, not the venue. A heavy cloth at a July valley reception is miserable by the first dance. Forgetting the shoes. Trouser length depends on the heel. Bring the actual pair to every fitting. Questions to ask your tailor Before you commit, ask these five questions. A good studio will answer each one in a sentence. When is my final fitting, relative to the date? It should be two to three weeks out. What happens if my weight changes before then? Look for generous seam inlays and a final-fitting adjustment. Which cloths suit my venue and month? The answer should mention weight in grams or ounces, not just colour. How are the groomsmen handled? Ask about measuring windows, deadlines and what happens if someone is late. Is the price confirmed in writing before cutting? It should be. If you’re short on time If your date is under three months away, talk to us anyway. /journal/executive-capsule-wardrobe.text: Home / Journal / Building an Executive Capsule Wardrobe Wardrobe Building an Executive Capsule Wardrobe By [PLACEHOLDER: founder full name ] , Founder & Head Clothier · October 19, 2026 · 8 min read In this article Why a capsule The core pieces Palette Cloth and climate Shirts, ties and details Dress codes in Utah business Travelling with the capsule Outerwear and knitwear What to retire The order to build it Keeping it sharp Key takeaways A working executive capsule is 15–20 core pieces built around navy and grey. Four suits is the practical minimum for daily wear, so each one rests between wears. Commission in order: navy suit, grey suit, odd jacket, then the second navy and grey. In Utah, plan two cloth weights: high-twist for summer, flannel for winter. The best-dressed executives rarely look like they have thought about clothes, because they thought about them once, properly, and then stopped. A capsule wardrobe is how that happens: a small, deliberate set of pieces that all work together, built to fit and maintained so nothing ever looks tired. Why a capsule Decision fatigue is real, and the morning is a poor time to spend it. A capsule removes the decision. Every jacket works with every trouser, and every shirt works with every suit. It also sends a consistent signal: the people you lead and the people you negotiate with see the same considered person every time. A capsule is also cheaper over time. Fewer, better pieces, rotated so each one rests, last far longer than a crowded wardrobe of near-misses. The core pieces A strong starting capsule for an executive who wears tailoring most days: Piece Quantity Why Navy suit 2 The most versatile colour in tailoring. One plain, one with a subtle texture or stripe. Grey suit 2 Mid-grey worsted for year-round wear, charcoal flannel for winter. Odd jacket 1–2 A navy hopsack or textured blazer for less formal days, and for travel. Trousers 3 Mid-grey, tan and a winter flannel, all wearable with the odd jacket. Shirts 8–10 White and pale blue. Spread collars for ties, a softer collar for open-neck wear. Knitwear 2–3 Fine merino in navy and grey, worn under a jacket on cold days. Overcoat 1 Mid-length, in navy or charcoal, cut to fit over a suit. Shoes 3 pairs Black oxfords, dark brown oxfords or derbies, and brown loafers. That’s roughly 15–20 core pieces of tailoring and outerwear, before shirts and shoes. Four suits is the practical minimum for daily wear, because rotating lets each suit rest at least a day between wears so the cloth recovers. Palette Build on navy and grey; they work with almost every complexion and every shirt. Add brown and tan through odd trousers, shoes and knitwear. Keep patterns quiet: a fine stripe, a subtle check or a textured weave reads as rich without being loud. Your best shades depend on your colouring, which is exactly what a colour analysis settles. Executives now spend much of their week on camera, so consider how cloth reads on a screen. Very fine stripes and tight herringbones can shimmer (moiré) on video, and pure black reads as a flat void under office lighting. Solid navy, textured grey and a light-blue shirt are the most dependable combination on screen and in person. Cloth and climate In Salt Lake City, plan for two seasons. From May to September, high-twist wools and fresco at 230–270 g breathe in dry heat and resist creasing on travel days. From October to April, flannels and heavier worsteds at 300–370 g are warmer and drape beautifully. A 270–300 g worsted bridges both and is the right weight for the first suit. Choose Super 100s–130s for daily suits; they outlast finer cloths. More detail is in our fabric guide . Shirts, ties and the details Shirts do most of the visible work. Two colours, white and pale blue, cover nearly every situation, and two collar shapes cover the rest: a spread collar that frames a tie knot, and a softer button-down or cutaway that stays neat when worn open. Choose ties in solid grenadine or fine repp in navy, burgundy and green, and they will work with every suit in the capsule. Keep the small things consistent: one belt and one pair of braces in each of black and brown, and a watch that slips under the cuff. Consistency reads as confidence. Dress codes in Utah business Utah’s business dress is, on average, less formal than in New York or London, and it varies sharply by sector. Law firms, courtrooms, banking and senior healthcare still expect a suit and tie. Much of the technology sector around Lehi and the Silicon Slopes runs business casual, where an odd jacket and open collar outrank a full suit. An executive capsule for Utah therefore leans more on odd jackets and trousers than a coastal one would, and keeps two or three suits ready for board meetings, investor days and court. Travelling with the capsule A well-built capsule packs into one carry-on for a three-day trip. Take a navy suit and a pair of grey odd trousers, which give you two looks from one jacket. Add three shirts, two ties and one pair of oxfords worn on the plane. High-twist cloth springs back from creasing overnight. To pack the jacket, turn one shoulder inside out and tuck the other into it, then fold once at the waist. Outerwear and knitwear for a Utah winter Salt Lake City winters are cold and bright, with snow on the benches and frequent inversions in the valley. The capsule needs a coat that goes over tailoring: a mid-length overcoat in navy or charcoal wool, or wool–cashmere, cut with enough room in the shoulder and sleeve to sit over a jacket without dragging. Add a lighter raincoat or a quilted layer for spring and autumn. Fine merino knitwear is the quiet workhorse. A navy or grey crew-neck under an odd jacket replaces a shirt and tie for informal days, and a thin roll-neck under a flannel suit is warm enough for an evening in Park City. Choose 12–16 gauge merino so it sits flat under tailoring. What to retire Building a capsule means editing as well as adding. Retire anything that fails the shoulder test, because a jacket that is wrong at the shoulder cannot be fixed. Retire suits shiny at the seat or elbows, and shirts with frayed collars. Let go of anything you haven’t worn in a year because “nothing goes with it”. A capsule’s whole premise is that everything goes with everything. What remains will be smaller, and you will wear all of it. The order to build it You don’t need to commission everything at once. A sensible sequence: Navy suit in a year-round worsted: the workhorse. Mid-grey suit : doubles your rotation and your options. Odd jacket and two trousers : unlock the less formal days. Second navy and charcoal flannel : complete the four-suit rotation. Overcoat : before your first Utah winter in the new wardrobe. Because the first bespoke suit establishes your pattern, every later piece starts from a proven fit. Keeping it sharp Rotate suits, and rest each one at least a day after wearing. Brush after wear and hang on broad, shaped hangers. Dry clean rarely. Press and spot-clean instead, because cleaning chemicals wear cloth down. Review the wardrobe each season, and repair or replace before anything looks tired. That seasonal review is the heart of our executive wardrobe programme.
